title: Passive vs Active Reconnaissance: The Line That Cannot Be Crossed
content:
Imagine you want to learn everything you can about a building.

Option A: You stand across the street, watch the comings and goings, read the company name on the sign, take note of which cars park there, search the company's name online, and look at the building on Google Maps Street View. You gather an enormous amount of information. Nobody inside the building knows you exist.

Option B: You walk up to the front door and ring the bell. Someone answers. You've just announced your presence.

This is the difference between passive and active reconnaissance — and it is one of the most important distinctions in all of professional security.

---

**Passive Reconnaissance**

Passive reconnaissance is gathering information about a target WITHOUT making any direct contact with the target's systems. You are observing. Reading. Searching public databases. Looking at what is already publicly available.

Key characteristic: the target cannot detect you. There are no logs. No alerts. No trace. You never touched their systems.

Examples of passive reconnaissance:
• Searching for the company's name on LinkedIn — learning the names and job titles of their employees
• Reading their job postings — discovering that they hire 'AWS engineers with Terraform experience' tells you their cloud infrastructure
• Looking up WHOIS records — public domain registration data that shows who owns a domain and when it was registered
• Checking SSL certificate logs (crt.sh) — publicly logged certificates that reveal subdomains
• Searching GitHub for the company's name — sometimes finding repositories with internal naming conventions, or accidentally committed credentials
• Using HaveIBeenPwned to check if the company's email domain appeared in a known data breach
• Looking at archived versions of their website on the Wayback Machine at archive.org

None of these actions touch the target's systems. None of them send a packet to the target. All of them gather real intelligence.

---

**Active Reconnaissance**

Active reconnaissance is gathering information about a target BY directly interacting with the target's systems. You are making contact. Sending packets. Requesting data. The target's servers are responding to your requests — and potentially logging your IP address while doing so.

Key characteristic: the target CAN detect you, because your activity creates a footprint in their logs.

Examples of active reconnaissance:
• Port scanning with Nmap — sending TCP probes to the target's IP address to see which ports are open
• Banner grabbing — sending a request to a service to see what version it returns in its response
• DNS zone transfer attempts — asking a target's DNS server for its complete record set
• Web crawling — sending HTTP requests to the target's web server to discover hidden paths and files
• SMTP enumeration — testing whether specific email addresses exist by observing how the target's mail server responds

Active reconnaissance belongs to a later stage of the engagement — and it requires explicit written authorisation in your scope agreement. This is the legal line. Passive reconnaissance on a company you have no contract with is generally legal (you are only reading public information). Active reconnaissance without written authorisation is computer fraud in most jurisdictions, regardless of your intent.

---

**The grey zone — and why it matters**

Some reconnaissance techniques sit on the boundary between passive and active.

Shodan — sometimes called 'the search engine for the internet' — continuously scans the entire public internet for devices and records what it finds. If you look up an IP address on Shodan, you are reading Shodan's cached data. That is passive: you are reading a database, not scanning the target. But if you trigger a new, fresh scan of a target on Shodan, packets are sent to the target. That is active.

Google's indexed results are passive — Google sent the crawl requests; you are reading what Google found. But if you visit the target's website directly, you are making contact — that is technically active, though generally considered acceptable within most scope agreements for public-facing web properties.

The rule of thumb for professionals: if the data came from someone else scanning the target, reading that data is passive. If you are the one making the request to the target, it is active.

---

**Why this distinction matters professionally**

In a real penetration testing engagement, you begin with passive reconnaissance and exhaust it fully before switching to active. The reason is both tactical and legal.

Tactically: passive reconnaissance builds a complete intelligence picture without alerting the target. If the organisation has a Security Operations Centre (SOC) watching for suspicious activity, they cannot see your passive reconnaissance. Active reconnaissance can trigger alerts — especially port scans, which modern intrusion detection systems identify immediately. Starting active before passive means potentially alerting the target before you have enough intelligence to act effectively.

Legally: passive reconnaissance on publicly available information does not require authorisation. Active reconnaissance against a specific target's systems does. Knowing exactly when you cross this line protects you and defines the boundaries of what your scope agreement covers.

callouts.title: The Legal Line
callouts.text: Passive reconnaissance using publicly available information is legal in virtually all jurisdictions — you are reading public data, not accessing private systems. Active reconnaissance against a specific target's systems without written authorisation is illegal under the Computer Misuse Act 1990 (UK), the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (US), and equivalent laws globally. Your intention does not change your legal exposure. 'I was just checking if the port was open to help them' is not a recognised legal defence.

callouts.title: A Practical Sequence
callouts.text:
Professional penetration testers follow this sequence:
1. Exhaust all passive OSINT sources completely
2. Organise and analyse what you have gathered
3. Identify which active techniques to use and against which specific targets
4. Confirm all active techniques are within the agreed scope
5. Begin active reconnaissance only once steps 1–4 are complete

This sequence means you arrive at the active phase with a precise understanding of what to look for — not a blank-slate scan of everything.

keyTerms.definition: Information gathering about a target using ONLY publicly available sources, with zero direct contact with the target's systems. The target cannot detect this activity because no packets are sent to their infrastructure. Examples: WHOIS lookups, LinkedIn research, job posting analysis, SSL certificate logs, breach databases.

Information gathering that involves directly interacting with the target's systems — sending packets, making requests, or querying the target's services. The target CAN detect this activity because their systems respond and may log the interaction. Examples: Nmap port scanning, banner grabbing, web crawling. Requires explicit written authorisation.

Open Source Intelligence. Intelligence gathered from publicly available sources: websites, social media, public records, news archives, certificate logs, and breach databases. The word 'open source' means publicly available — not 'open source software'. OSINT is always passive by definition.

The record of activity left behind when interacting with a target's systems. Active reconnaissance creates a footprint in the target's logs (your IP address, timestamps, the requests made). Passive reconnaissance creates no footprint on the target — though public OSINT activities may be logged by the services you use (Google, LinkedIn, Shodan).
